Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Vignette:
Kwame had spent thirty-eight years in the high-bay chemical disposal facility, but the day the pressurized solvent tank ruptured still played out behind his eyes with startling clarity. He was recalibrating the extraction arm when a hydraulic valve blew with a sharp, concussive crack that shook the concrete floor. A white plume of toxic mist rolled through the aisle, stinging his eyes and burning his throat. He remembered gripping the metal railing, his palms slick with sweat, as the emergency alarms shrieked and the heavy blast doors hissed shut, sealing him in the swirling cloud until the ventilation system finally cleared the air. The treatment began immediately at the on-site clinic, where the sharp tang of antiseptic wipes and the crisp paper of the examination table became deeply woven into his recovery. In the months that followed, the clinic’s antiseptic smell followed him into everyday life. A whiff of cleaning solution in the grocery aisle or the faint chemical bite of his wife’s laundry detergent would make his chest tighten, pulling him back to that sealed aisle and the burning air. Back at the workplace, the routine hum of the ventilation fans and the sudden clatter of a dropped wrench triggered the same tightness. He found himself constantly scanning the high-ceilinged bay, his eyes tracking the overhead pipes, the safety placards, and the positions of the exit doors. He had come to believe that comfort arrived only when he could map every possible way out. When his wife or a colleague approached from behind and laid a hand on his shoulder, he would flinch, his shoulders rising toward his ears before he realized it was only a familiar gesture. The startle did not fade; it simply became a routine part of his day, as constant as the shift whistle. His scanning for danger and his habit of tracing escape routes unfolded side by side, each occupying his attention in the bay and beyond, without one leading to the other. Kwame avoided being alone in rooms or buildings. His avoidance and his overwork developed as parallel habits, each occupying his days. He lingered in the facility’s lobby or walked the perimeter of the loading dock long after his shift ended. He began taking on extra maintenance rounds and staying late to calibrate the decompression chambers. His wife noticed how he packed the guest room with boxes over the years, leaving the master bedroom feeling less like a shared space and more like a place he merely passed through. He also postponed routine physical examinations, steering clear of hospitals and ambulances unless absolutely necessary, wary of the bright lights, the clinical smells, and the sudden proximity of medical staff. His check-ups became careful negotiations, scheduled around his own terms and kept to a minimum. Avoidance of medical cues and his habit of staying late in the workplace ran through his life as separate, steady currents. At sixty-two, Kwame’s work had slowed to a steady, deliberate pace, yet the old vigilance remained. He still mapped the exit routes in every new room, still flinched when a heavy door slammed, still found himself breathing through his mouth when the facility’s solvent drums were moved. The accumulation of these quiet habits had finally drawn him to seek help. His wife had gently placed his PCL-5 score of 57 on the kitchen table, noting how his nights had grown shorter and how he sometimes stood by the bedroom window long after she fell asleep, watching the streetlights and the distant highway. He was uncertain about what lay ahead, unsure whether the world would ever feel truly breathable again, but he had come to the clinic hoping to find a way to live without constantly bracing for the next sharp sound, the next sudden breath of chemical air, or the next unexpected touch.
